summary: Poland is part of the EU and the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (with the ETIAS travel authorization being phased in), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

source.name: European Commission — Schengen short-stay calculator (DG Migration and Home Affairs)

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since June 11, 2024.
For stays over 90 days within a year: work, study, family and other long-stay purposes. Some categories are reduced or exempt.
For courses longer than 90 days; needs proof of enrollment at a Polish institution, funds and health insurance.
Requires a work permit or a declaration of entrustment of work obtained by the employer in Poland before the visa application.

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

proofOfFunds.text: Poland sets a minimum means requirement for non-EU visitors: 75 PLN per person per day for stays over 4 days, or a total of 300 PLN for stays up to 4 days (plus funds for the return journey).

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.
Extra checks apply on the external borders with Belarus, Russia and Ukraine. Some crossings are closed or restricted.

payments.text: Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere, and the local BLIK mobile payment system is ubiquitous. Cash is rarely needed outside small markets.

safety.text: Poland is one of Europe's safest destinations, with low violent crime. Watch for pickpocketing on public transport in Warsaw and Kraków and avoid unlicensed taxis.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Poland Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–September brings warm weather for cities, the Baltic coast and the Tatra mountains; December adds atmospheric Christmas markets in Kraków and Wrocław.

idp.text: Poland is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Poland is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Poland yet.

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just Poland — days spent in Germany or Czechia count against the same allowance.
Use ride-hailing apps (Uber, Bolt, FreeNow) or clearly marked licensed taxis with a rate card — unlicensed taxis touting at airports and stations heavily overcharge.
First-time EES biometric registration can add wait time at airports. Arrive with margin on your first Schengen entry.
Always choose to pay in złoty (PLN), not your home currency, at card terminals and ATMs — dynamic currency conversion adds a poor exchange rate.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Poland?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Poland and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a Poland Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across all Schengen countries, and applications are decided within 15–45 calendar days.

faq.question: Can Ukrainian citizens enter Poland without a visa?
faq.answer: Yes, holders of Ukrainian biometric passports can enter visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Ukrainians who fled the war are covered by separate special protection arrangements that allow longer stay and access to work. Check current Polish government rules before relying on them.

faq.question: Does Poland use the euro?
faq.answer: No. Poland uses the Polish złoty (PLN). Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere, so you rarely need much cash; when paying by card, always choose to be charged in PLN.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Poland without a visa?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt non-EU visitors can stay up to 90 days within any 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area. EU and EFTA citizens can stay indefinitely but must register locally after 3 months.
